topic: Te Here ā Nuku (Nelson Tenths) Bill
description: Wednesday 8 July 2026 | Finance and Expenditure Committee Te Here ā Nuku (Nelson Tenths) Bill Rangitane o Wairau Group Corey Hebberd, General Manager Nelson Marlborough Fish and Game Council New Zealand Fish and Game Council Bill O'Leary, Deputy Chair Rhys Barrier, Regional Manager Rachael Ennor, Legal Counsel Daniel Jackson Pacific Eco-Logic Victoria Froude
descriptionSummary: Te Here ā Nuku (Nelson Tenths) Bill. Rangitane o Wairau Group. Corey Hebberd, General Manager

chunks.text: Yep. See you guys. Where'd you go? Kia ora. Rangitane Tangata Rau, Rangitane Nui, Rangitane Whitu ki te rangi ko Rangitane ki te whenua. Tena tatou katoa. E hoa tatou tenni mate. O tera i tenei kaupapa a tatou. Kia ora, members. My name is Corey Hebbert. I'm the General Manager for Rangitane Owairu, joined by Dr Peter Meihana, who is both a trustee of Rangitane Owairu and the Te Hiri Anuku Trust.

Mm-hmm. Before we begin, just want to acknowledge the significant weather events affecting Te Tauihu in the past 24 hours, and particularly our whanaungia in Kaikōura to the south. There's been significant flooding, road closures, and disruptions, so our thoughts with everyone in the region. Kia ora. I also want to acknowledge Matawaroari Stafford and his whānau. The fact that this bill is before you today reflects decades of effort by many people, with Matawaroari central to ensuring that this matter continues to progress towards its final resolution.

Rangitane Owairu supports the Te Hiri Anuku Nelson Tents Bill. While Rangitane is not a direct beneficiary under the legislation or the resolution agreement, many of our whānau descend from tūpuna connected to the Nelson Tents lands and the wider history behind this grievance. The Nelson Tents issue has been examined extensively through litigation, historical research, Crown engagement, and negotiation.

The history is well known, the findings are well documented, and the Crown has acknowledged that obligations associated with the Tents reserves were not honored as originally intended. This committee is not being asked to determine whether a grievance exists. The question that is before you is whether effect should now be given to the resolution agreement reached between Te Hiri Anuku Trust and the Crown through this bill.

We believe it should. This resolution is significant not only because it resolves matters arising from the Nelson Tents litigation, but because it enables the Crown to complete commitments that have already been made, including aspects of Treaty settlement redress that have remained unresolved as a consequence of that litigation. Auckland Point School in Nelson provides a useful example.

The school forms part of the Rangitane Owairu Treaty settlement. Rangitane exercised its right to purchase the property in March 2015 and has since been the beneficial owner. However, legal title could not transfer because the property remained subject to a caveat associated with the Nelson Tents litigation and lands within the Spain Award area. As a result, Treaty settlement redress that had already been agreed could not be fully implemented by the Crown.

Following the resolution agreement reached in December last year, the Crown confirmed that the redress can proceed as originally intended. The lifting of the caveat has enabled the transfer process to move forward and removed uncertainty that has existed since the time of our settlement. Auckland Point School is just one example, but it demonstrates that the consequences of the Nelson Tents litigation extended beyond the lands directly affected by the proceedings.

This bill does more than transfer land and assets to Te Hiri Anuku Trust. It implements the resolution agreement. It gives effect to court findings. It provides certainty regarding property and governance arrangements within Te Tauihu, and it enables longstanding Treaty settlement commitments to also finally be completed. The resolution agreement signed on the 17th of December 2025 was the product of extensive negotiation between Te Hiri Anuku and the Crown.

Parliament now has the opportunity to give effect to that agreement. I also wish to briefly address the inclusion of the Kura Haupo tūpuna, as this has been raised by some submitters. Rangitane's support for this bill is consistent with the findings of the Waitangi Tribunal and the Crown's own acknowledgments. The Tribunal found that Rangitane tūpuna and Kura Haupo tūpuna should have been beneficiaries of the Nelson Tents reserve, while the Crown has acknowledged that Rangitane did not receive a share of those reserves.

This matter forms part of the historical record and provides important context for the inclusion of those Kura Haupo tūpuna. I also note public concerns regarding future access arrangements. Those concerns, we believe, should be viewed in context. This legislation relates to land that the courts found was held by the Crown on trust for descendants of the customary owners.

Te Hiri Anuku Trust has committed to maintaining existing arrangements for at least 25 years and has stated that future arrangements will be guided by principles of partnership, kaitiakitanga, and stewardship. In our view, that should provide confidence to the committee and to the public that this bill is about implementing a negotiated resolution, not about restricting public access.

In summary, the Nelson Tents grievance is longstanding and is well documented, and it has already been extensively examined. This bill gives effect to the resolution agreement reached between Te Hiri Anuku Trust and the Crown. Auckland Point School demonstrates how the litigation affected wider Crown Treaty settlement commitments, including our own Treaty settlement redress.

This bill enables longstanding settlement commitments to be completed and provides certainty for the future. Parliament now has the opportunity to implement the agreed resolution through this legislation. For those reasons, Rangitane Owairu supports the bill and respectfully encourages the committee to recommend that it proceed.

In closing, I want to place on record Rangitane's acknowledgments to Dr Peter Meihana and Nicole Akuhaza for their work on behalf of the three Kura Haupo iwi and our people, the trustees of Te Hiri Anuku Trust, the many whānau who have supported this kaupapa over many years, and former Attorney General Honorable Judith Collins and the Crown officials involved in reaching the resolution agreement.

Finally, I again want to acknowledge Matawaroari Stafford and his whānau, whose longstanding commitment, and indeed sacrifice, has been instrumental to bringing the matter to this point. Mr Chair, we're happy to take any questions with the time remaining. Thank you. A very clear submission. We've got Dan Rosewarne. Yeah. Hey, thanks, Corey, for that detailed submission.

You spoke about the history, the shared history of Te Tauihu iwi within your submission, and I was just wondering what opportunities do you see this bill creating for future collaboration between the descendants of the customary owners and the wider iwi within the region? Sure. So to tell you who has a rich tapestry of whakapapa, many of us whakapapa are across the multiple iwi within the region.

I myself, across the nine iwi of Te Waipounamu, whakapapa to nine. Pete, I think you whakapapa to most. So already there's existing collaborations through existing treaty settlement arrangements and the like, where we do work collaboratively and constructively together. The eight iwi collaborate in a multi-vehicle trust and other mechanisms. So I see this very much as continuing the work that has gone on before, but importantly, enabling completion of those outstanding matters in respect of the Nelson tents, which of course have been

longstanding matters unresolved outside of treaty settlement processes. But certainly provides a really strong footing that gives effect to some of those aspirations that I know our people would have had at the time of the tents being formed. Thanks, Corey. Thanks, Dan. Steve Abel.

Oh, sorry, just found my audio button. Thank you very much for that substantive and really clear submission. Can you give us a bit more detail on the specific Auckland School issue, and how the passage of this bill resolves that? Sure. So Auckland Point School was a deferred settlement property within the Rangitane settlement. We passed our settlement in August 2014, and then had the option to exercise a right of first refusal to purchase land at Auckland Point School. Due to the Stafford litigation, there was a caveat placed on the school by Wakatu Incorporation at the time, as it was

advancing proceedings on behalf of the customary owners. As a result of the resolution agreement having been reached, and as a result of this legislation now moving through its passage, that's given the ability for that caveat to be lifted and for the Crown to take steps to transfer legal title of that property through to Rangitane. It has been prevented from doing that to date, which means that that treaty settlement commitment has been unable to be put into place.

And so this enables, obviously, the intent of our treaty settlement commitments and the Crown to fulfill its obligations to transfer legal title consistent with the original intent. Okay, brilliant. Thank you. Thank you both for your submission. Very clear and, yeah, great to have something so supportive as well. Appreciate your time today.
Members, we're now going to go to the Nelson Marlborough Fish and Game Council. We've also got them for 10 minutes.

Good morning, team, or afternoon. Morning. They're those on? Yep. Good morning, everyone. Tena koutou, tena koutou katoa. My name's Bill O'Leary, I'm the deputy chair with Nelson Marlborough Fish and Game, and be presenting alongside with the national council. So with me at the moment, we have got Carina Jordan, who is the CEO of the New Zealand Council.

We've also got, probably listening in, Richie Cosgrove, who is our operations manager. And alongside me, I have got, on one side, I've got Reece, who is our ops manager here in our Nelson Marlborough area, and we're supported by Rachel, who is a barrister.

Sorry, just a brief technical point. The Nelson Marlborough Council and the New Zealand Council are seeking the committee's leave to present together. They each have 10-minute slots as organizations. If it is with the committee's leave, Mr. Chair, wonder if the clerk could allow the national office onto this call as panelists at this point as well, so that they can participate in the full 20 minutes along with the Nelson Marlborough- Okay. They are the next submitter anyways, isn't that right, ma'am?

Yeah. Slot, that's right. Any objections, members? No, that sounds fine. Thank you. I would encourage you, even though you've got 20 minutes, save some time for questions because with both of you, it does tend to go fast, so Thank you. Thank you. We acknowledge those people who are listening in, particularly any members of the trust that may be listening.

We're extremely supportive of the bill and extremely supportive of the process by which the wrongs of the past may be set right. I'd like to put a little personal note in on this one at this stage. I spent 35 years teaching senior history here in Nelson.

It was New Zealand history with a big emphasis on what was happening at a local level, and it was fairly well impossible to operate in that particular field without an awareness of the situation that the tents people had found themselves in.

We were supported at that stage by the academic input from John Mitchell and Hillary, and that gave us a background, but also in my past, had the experience of studying with Harry Evison, who would be very, very well known to anyone who has looked at the Kempth purchase history.

So with that personal background, I would like to actually emphasize the fact that I personally am extremely supportive of this legislation. The submissions that the two councils have put in have been lodged with reluctance We know that the legislation is designed to set right a wrong.

The situation that we find ourselves in is that as a third party, we have been affected, and the legislation as it stands and the process that seems to be there is that it would have a negative impact on us.

You will have read our submissions, so therefore there's no intention of simply re-litigating or going over those again. Nelson Marlborough Fish and Game, in its present situation, is at Champion Road in Richmond, Nelson. We've been here for 60-odd years.

Originally, it was a gravel reserve, and as a reserve, we had the authority to operate on it and to utilise it for our statutory purposes under the various legislation, both Conservation Act and also the Fish and Game legislation. Today, what was a gravel reserve has now got a building on it, and it's surrounded totally by residential areas.

The area has changed. We understand that the ground is being passed back to the trust, and we've been advised only very recently, a matter of two and a half months ago, that the building, the assets that we have established here on this land, will follow the land itself into the possession of the trust.

From our point of view, that means that as a organisation, as a statutory body, we will be losing not necessarily the control, but certainly the ownership of those assets, and that will have a significant effect on our operations potentially, but most certainly on our financial situation.

Fish and Game, as I'm sure you are aware, operates entirely from the licenses and the income from the licenses of people who go fishing and game bird hunting. We operate on the smell of an oily rag. We'd like to think that we-- We do know that we operate very effectively and efficiently, and the effect of the loss of an asset here, and perhaps the necessity for us to relocate, if not immediately,

then certainly perhaps in the longer term, that's going to create significant problems for us. We're faced here with the problem that the legislation, while it appears to protect party rights, or rather the rights of third parties, in our particular case, we have real difficulty.

We'd like to have been able to have sorted this out with the Crown directly, because we believe it is the Crown's responsibility to look after and to protect the interests of a third party. However, because we've not been able to make progress in this particular field, it's necessary for us to make the submission, and in effect, lodge our concern.

Putting all the legal side to one side, because I will leave that to our barrister, the situation is we've been here for 60-odd years. The reserve purpose that was here was for us to function and for this land to be used for the purposes of acclimatisation, which progressed to the movement of fish and game, and that's what we do. We look after the resource, which is the freshwater fish, the game birds of this area.

And when I say of this area, I'm talking about an area from effectively to the north of Karamea, coming around through Golden Bay, the Tasman area, the whole of Marlborough, and all the way down to Kaikoura. A very large area, and we administer it and look after the resource there.

We also look after our members. We've upgraded the facilities that we needed, a headquarters building, a garage. All of this has been done at the expense of the license holders, and the money has the construction of those taken absolutely no input from government or from any other agency.

It's funded totally by license holders. Everything that we've done has been authorised by the Crown and by the local authorities. So we've complied with the requirements of legislation, the requirements of regulation, and we have been what we would consider to be effective and lawful people operating the business that we were set up to do.

The improvements that we're looking at here are in the vicinity of about $730,000 to $800,000. A significant amount of money for people that, and an organization that is funded totally by license holders. We need some arrangement that will enable us to be recompensed for the loss, so that we can continue the work that we are set up to do.

That's your 10 minutes. Okay. That's your 10 minutes. Thank you. Yeah. Righto. Thank you, Bill. I'll answer legal questions as they come up from committee members, perhaps rather than setting out the legal position. However, just in a very quick essence of it, Clause 109 of the bill states that third party rights will continue, and it works very effectively for real property.

That is clearly and unambiguously a right in property that can be registrable, et cetera. In this situation, things are a little bit more in the territory of potentially they own the improvements, but that might be more in common law, equity, rights in personam, those sorts of matters.

So the view is that there's definitely a legal interest here, but it's not a nice clean legal interest that can be put on a property title and registered in favor of these folks. So they're left in a little bit of a gray patch, and at the moment, Section 109 says that it those, but it's not clear how. So I'll be available for questions after.

Carina may want to make just a couple of comments first. I'm super cognizant of time, so Morena. Just wanted to reiterate that the New Zealand Fish and Game Council is strongly supportive of the historic resolution agreement reached by the trust and the Crown, and that agreement's implementation through Te Here Anauku Nelson Tenants Bill. So the matters raised in the submission relate solely to the obligations of the Crown under the Bill and in no way reflect on the settlement itself or the trust.

We've got strong working relationships, which we're going to work to retain. And so what we're trying to do here is just address challenges in relation to an asset and its improvements in relation to the cost of the organization, which is completely funded by license holders. And we're hoping to work with the Crown outside of this process to try and resolve these matters, and I'll open the floor for questions.

Thanks. I might just kick off with one. Regarding, I think in the submissions there was a figure of $800,000. So is this a perceived risk of asset value, or rather it's just the uncertainty surrounding how it might happen in terms of the property shifting ownership?

Is it about access? Just sort of seeking what is it more specifically you're looking to clarify. There is a lot that is unknown, and the council are willing to meet the costs of some of the changes. They're moving from being here in perpetuity in their own right to being a tenant of the landlords that are Te Here Anauku Trust, and they don't have a problem with that. They think that's fair, right, and just in the context of all of this. But where they draw the line is the loss of substantial financial assets or a substantial financial cost to them

from that. So the $800,000, Mr. Chair, has been estimated. There's a replacement, evaluation replacement for insurance purposes been assessed at $730 for the improvements on this land. And that's been rounded up to $800,000 in that they're having to meet legal costs of me right now trying to advocate for them, and we don't know what other costs may come in time.

There's likely to be an income stream required. We don't know yet whether they will actually have to be relocated from this land or not. But even if they do stay on the land, it will be as tenants, not as owners of this improvement. And if they leave the land, they can't take the building with them. So there's an issue there of real value for them or for the trust. So probably the most constructive thing is for them to be compensated now. It becomes the trust property free and clear, and everybody moves on into the future in a way that Te Here Anauku and this council agree between

themselves under the Act. Thank you. Question from Steve Abel. So squarely, the issue's with the way the Crown manages its obligations to you as a third party. Yeah. And the gap between the obligation to fulfill third party rights and the diminishment of asset value that might be affected by the bill becoming an act and put into force. That's the gap that you want the Crown to have an answer for.

That's right, Steve. Yeah. And I think, arguably they already have that obligation. But it's certainly not clear, and the direct experience of these folks has been that it's been very difficult to protect- To identify and to protect their third party interest here, because it's not as cut and clear as maybe would've been ideal. But they've done nothing wrong.

They've been here for 60 plus years, done what they were required to do by Parliament as a Fish and Game council here, and built these buildings because they needed these buildings to be able to do that work that they have to do. So, they've done absolutely nothing wrong. And the asset's been on their books all the time, not on DOC's asset register, for instance. So it's a bit of a legal, quirky thing, and there's a bit of a gap there.

And there may be value in the committee just clarifying that any third party interests, the sub-clauses two and three of Section 109, I think work very well for real property, that clear interest in land that can be registered. They work less well for this kind of interest, which may be equitable or in common law or some other flavor.

Is there a council quick sub, Mr. Chair? Yeah. And I guess there's a risk that if it's not resolved by the Crown early or ahead of time, of placing the burden of that loss that you are feeling or may feel onto the relationship with Te Here Anauku, which would be unjust for both yourselves and Te Here Anauku.

Absolutely. And I think there is an argument under that Section 109 that that's exactly what happens, is that any interest in the land, which this is, as I say, a bit gray, travel with the land in that way, including perhaps some obligation to these guys to pay them out at some point. So I think everybody has been constructive and proactive here and wants to sort it out- Mm.

Yeah. Okay... outside of this. But yeah, you've understood the issue perfectly. Yeah, very clear. Thank you. Thank you. Dr. David Wilson. Thank you, Chair. Earlier on I asked this question, were there any third party interested property rights involved in this transaction? To which the answer was no. That's clearly not correct.

No. That's one thing. And you said that under Clause 109 that's a gray area, and I completely understand that. My question really goes to this, because it seems like there was goodwill there for these sorts of things to be negotiated. And my question is, in terms of the activities, you maintaining your activities, why is it difficult to maintain those activities, albeit possibly with the transfer of ownership of land and buildings?

There will have been a substantial financial reduction in the assets of this council. Yeah. And they will still have to run with $800,000 less on their asset sheet than they currently have. Yeah. They're already on a smell of an oily rag, so that would be the direct implication in that way. There's a lot that's already unknown.

Just in relation to your first comment, Section 109, I think the policy is very clear that any third party rights are not meant to be affected by this. And I think that is what has been agreed between the Crown and Te Here Anauku in all good faith, and I think that is the policy intent. I just think at the moment there's a slight gap in achieving that policy intent with the current drafting.

So the answer you received earlier of any effect on third party rights, I'd refer you to Clause 109 subsection one. There's a clear statement there that third party rights will continue. The complications come, as we've already discussed, where it's a little less clear.

Supplementary, Chair. Yeah. It sort of seems in the way that you're presenting this, that you've made the assumption that you need to leave, and that the activities you've been doing for the last 60 years can't continue. Is that correct? I think there's not an absolute assumption of that, and I think the trust and the local council who here have a really good working relationship and anticipate that continuing in the future. So they'll work it out together.

But let's be real about it. At one point this was out in the country. It's now a highly valuable site, maybe for a future marae, maybe for a future development, whatever. It's Te Here Anauku's land, and they're entitled to do what they want with it over time. Whatever they do, these guys have trust that they'll do it in a fair, timely, reasonable manner.

But yeah, there's a possibility that they may have to move off the land. At the moment, that's only a possibility. If they do stay on the land, there's different commercial implications for them anyway. And there's no contemplation that they'd have to move off the land soon or even in the medium term probably, but it's a real thing for the potential long term, and I think we need to have our eyes open to that.

Thank you very much. Seems like an unresolved issue to me, Chair. Yeah. Thanks. Thanks, David. And just a final one from me on that. So notwithstanding everything you've said, your submission is very clear. It's not an immediate cash flow issue, it's more of an asset balance sheet, property holding. Would that be fair?

Yes, in relation to the asset, but no, in relation to the change from being their own administrator/controller manager to being a tenant. They assume, and they haven't yet negotiated with Te Here Anauku as to what Te Here Anauku may think are reasonable terms to be continuing on this site.

But there's an assumption that there may be some revenue required for Te Here Anauku and their beneficiaries. Yeah. And that's not currently budgeted for or planned or was never anticipated. Okay. So there is a potential direct financial cash flow issue in that. Yeah. No, appreciate that. The key issue is the asset one for these guys. Okay. No, we're going to have to wrap up there. Thank you very much.

Marlborough Fish and Game, and Fish and Game, was it Nelson as well? New Zealand Fish and Game Council, sorry. Thank you very much, Carina and team. And no doubt the process will take that into consideration. Kia ora. Kia ora. Members, we're now going to go to a personal submission in the name of Daniel Jackson.

Kia ora koutou. Kia ora, Daniel. We've only got you for five minutes, so please allow some time for questions if you like. We'll take your report as read, submission as read. Yes. Thank you. Kia ora koutou. I'm a resident in Nelson. I grew up here. I grew up hearing about the injustices and the history of the Nelson tents, so I'm very pleased to see that a resolution has been reached to the long-running litigation here, which, as a lawyer, I've followed over the years.

I'm also someone who has spent a fair bit of time in Abel Tasman National Park. I'm a tramper. I've been there many times, and I care a lot about the conservation in that area. So I support the bill, and I wanted to comment on the concerns that have been raised around Abel Tasman National Park and the bill. My view is that the bill doesn't need changes there, and that the concerns around Abel Tasman National Park are overstated. In

particular, I think it's important to note that the trust here has been clear that it's committed to conservation and kaitiakitanga. There's been very productive partnerships in Te Taihu, including in Abel Tasman National Park, between iwi, between mana whenua and other stakeholders, government, councils, NGOs, and volunteers, all contributing to conservation of the area.

And my view is that actually returning land within Abel Tasman National Park to the rightful owners should not be seen in any way as a threat to the conservation of this very important area. And that we all want the same thing here. We all want conservation of this area, and actually returning this land to the rightful owners to act as kaitiaki of it is a positive step here.

So as someone who loves Abel Tasman National Park, has spent lots of time here, and has always followed the history of the tents and this injustice, I see this as something that's actually really positive, and won't threaten the important conservation values of the area. So that's basically the key point I wanted to make, and I'll leave some time for questions.

Fantastic. We've got time for a quick question from Steve Abel. Yeah, I think no one could deny your absolute commitment to the value of conservation, Daniel, and you're just wanting to allay any public concerns that this agreement, this bill, is a threat to it, because you're confident that Te Heri o Ngaku will uphold their kaitiakitanga obligations and protect those conservation values.

Yeah. That's essentially the point. And we've seen mana whenua in the area very much participating as key stakeholders and key participants in a lot of the conservation partnerships and activity that's been occurring in Abel Tasman. And so I think that the idea that their ownership of the land is going to be a threat to conservation is sort of belied by the reality we've seen here.

And I think we should see this as actually an exciting opportunity and a next stage for the area, and not see returning the land to the rightful owners as a danger, but as an opportunity. Thank you, Daniel. A very clear submission. Appreciate that.
Thank you. We're now going to move to Victoria from Pacific Eco Logic. Welcome, Victoria. We've got you for 10 minutes, but of course, leave some time for questions if you like.

Kia ora. Tēnā koutou katoa. I'm a director of Pacific Eco Logic, and we used to operate out of Wellington, but now have moved to Bay of Islands. And as my submission, or the company submission indicated, we, me in particular, are very familiar with the area.

And from a work perspective, we map the coastal natural character for Tasman Coast, as well as we've been exploring that area for many years by boat, foot, kayak, and other mechanisms. I wanted to firstly just note we're ecologists, as the name applies, and note that the coastal section of Abel Tasman National Park, including the coastal track, is unique in New Zealand in the sense that it's easy topography, safe sandy beaches, equable conditions most

of the time, and you've got walkable sandy estuaries And another special feature for most of our national parks is we have the intensive invasive predator and plant pest control, which should increase the naturalness of the area over time. And there are some special areas, including the nature forest walk just north of Top Tenui Beach and the coastal ecosystems around Separation Point.

And we'd just note that it's also popular with overseas tourists because you've got more of the open vistas and it's not too rugged. So we noticed that looking at the bill there seemed to be some sections that appeared to us to be contradictory, or just unclear. So it was a bit ambiguous between different sections as to what actually is the provision.

And there were some missing and incorrect words. Now we've noted some of those in the submission, but there are others which should be picked up for clarity. We did obviously think that the time for consultation was very short, although I know the process has been going on for many years, and that it would be really helpful to have a public map showing the boundaries in a way that is more easily seen and understood by the public than is what obviously available online at this stage.

I don't want to go through the details of my submission or our submission. Just to note a couple of key points that we were looking for in decisions, and it was really that the national park status be retained in perpetuity for that Park of Abel Tasman that's been transferred into Te Hereke Nuku National Park.

And we're obviously keen that the scenic reserve status for shall be retained. That the coastal walk continue beyond 25 years so that that actually be part of the package. And we'd like to see provision for ongoing animal and plant pest control, consistent with what's happening on both sides, with funding to ensure that happens, and retain public access across the whole area as occurs at present. And we discussed the Waiporopupu Springs in the submission and just saying that we'd like to see the reserve

status be retained for that very special area. We do note that the water conservation order is being retained. So we just wanted to note that as a sort of a context in the background, that there is a big obligation on the Department of Conservation to keep up with what the $21 million of private Project Jansoon funding has achieved.

And we're just uncertain how we've got to the point where we've had this intensive work for projects being handed over from Project Jansoon back to the Department of Conservation, how that will be affected over time in terms of resourcing and the ongoing pest plant and animal control.

And also there seemed in our minds some question as to how long the DOC license would last for. There's provision for it to be 25 years, but it seemed like that could be reduced and again, how that sort of plays out in terms of resourcing and outcomes over time.

So, just to summarize, we'd like to thank you for the opportunity to comment to a place that's very dear to our hearts and hopes that the committee addresses the comments and points and concerns that we've raised in our submission. Thank you.

Thank you, Victoria. We've got a question from Steve Abel. Kia ora. Thank you, Victoria and acknowledging the amazing efforts and investment, and successes of Project Jansoon and the likes of yourself and your passion for protecting the biodiversity values and the amazing characteristics of Abel Tasman.

Would it not be correct to say that those of us who are passionate about our national parks and protecting biodiversity would equally say that the Department of Conservation may be under-resourced and may have failed in its success in protecting biodiversity as well as it could have? And that isn't that challenge a challenge that goes to any caretaker or owner of that biodiversity, and it may well be that Te Hereke Nuku will do a better job or will be more effective in its execution of those broader obligations to the commons,

if you like, to that extraordinary inheritance of biodiversity. And really your concern that there's an ability to have that dialogue and relationship with the new owners, who after all are the true owners, if you like. The court has rightly found that the Crown never had the right to create the national park in the way that it did because the land in fact was held in trust.

But in correcting that injustice, wouldn't it be another injustice to force an obligation of in perpetuity on to what is now deemed private land. Well, I think the submission in particular referred to not the department, but the Project Janszoon funding, which has made gains.

Yes. No, I acknowledge that. No, great gains, and well done. Yeah. So it was really how collectively we were going to continue and advance on those gains. So we weren't saying that there should be no transfer of ownership. It was just keen to protect the benefits achieved so far and ensuring that those continue.
